claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in multilayer HEA protective coatings is governed by nanoscale engineered interfaces.
Misfit at coherent or semi-coherent multilayer interfaces creates local strain fields.
Interface-associated local strain fields impede dislocation motion.
Homogeneous HEA coatings can serve as a monolithic comparison to multilayer HEA coatings.
The multilayer and monolithic coatings should be fabricated from the same overall HEA composition.
The baseline should have the same processing history as the multilayer coating.
Constant-stress loading at elevated temperature activates creep mechanisms.
An inert atmosphere suppresses extrinsic oxidation effects during the proposed creep comparison.
Multilayer interfaces trap, deflect, or delay dislocation glide.
Multilayer interfaces delay dislocation climb.
Delayed dislocation glide and climb reduce the accumulation of plastic strain under sustained loading.
Multilayer coatings should exhibit a significantly lower creep rate than homogeneous coatings.
Multilayer coatings should accumulate less time-dependent plastic strain than homogeneous coatings.
Dislocation pile-ups or deflections should be observed at multilayer interfaces after creep testing.
The proposed interface-barrier effect applies only while temperature, stress, and test duration preserve interface chemistry and structure.
Interdiffusion or oxidation can degrade the interfaces and invalidate the proposed effect.
The qualitative interface-barrier mechanism is supported by current evidence.
The magnitude of creep reduction and its dependence on layer thickness and interface coherence remain undetermined.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant creep-rate reduction would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe greater dislocation trapping or deflection at multilayer interfaces would falsify the hypothesis.
